1. Realized portfolio value

Three books that all start at the same dollar: the curated one, a buy-and-hold of the starter_watchlist (AAPL, GOOGL, AMZN) bought equal-dollar on day 1 and never touched, and SPY. Squares mark the weekly rebalances — dark red where an event actually opened or closed, orange where the curator rebalanced but changed nothing. Over this window the curated book ended at $277,153, the starter basket at $105,735, SPY at $90,975 — curating beat the starter basket and SPY. Kept OUT of the headline on purpose: a backtest steered by returns on known history is how you overfit, which is why this page leads with breadth and precision.

2. Watchlist composition over time

One row per ticker. The pale bar is the span the curator kept it WATCHLISTED — it held the thesis; the solid bar is the span the optimizer actually FUNDED it. The gap between them is the honest part: a name the curator believed in and the math never backed. Colour is the ticker’s dominant BEAT — which part of the firehose its evidence came from. Grey means no beat-attributable evidence.

3. Event timeline

The 143 events that RAN. The pale bar spans proposed → terminated; the solid overlay is when the optimizer actually FUNDED it, coloured by beat. A bar with no solid section is a thesis the curator held and the math never backed. Two classes are not drawn, and both are counted in panel 4: 0 events with no agent read at all, and 36 that opened and terminated on the SAME curation — those draw as hairlines indistinguishable from the axis and would bury the theses that ran.

4. Live events vs the cap

Theses the curator tracked at once, split by whether the optimizer put capital behind them, against the max_events ceiling (dashed). The stack’s top edge is the live count — where it touches the dashed line the cap is binding and the lowest coverage-ranked event was retired to make room, so the knob rather than the news set what got tracked. The amber band is the allocation bottleneck: live theses the math never backed, and across the run 107 of 179 events with an agent read died never funded. The dotted line is a flow, not part of the stack — events opened and closed in a single curation, dropped from panel 3 as hairlines.

5. Cumulative $ gain per holding

The 16 best and 8 worst funded names, with every other name rolled into one grey bar. A result resting on one or two names is a different thing from the same return spread across many — and the difference is not visible in the equity curve above. Click any named bar for that ticker’s price history, with ▲/▼ marking the moments the optimizer funded and unfunded it.

6. Cumulative $ gain per beat

The same dollars as the panel above, rolled up to the BEAT that surfaced each ticker’s evidence — i.e. which part of the firehose paid. A beat that costs money is a retrieval-vocabulary problem, not a curator one.

7. Gain per article read, by beat

The same dollars divided by how many of that beat's articles actually REACHED THE SCOUT — i.e. survived the discovery gate. That is the cost that binds: the scout is 91% of the LLM bill and reads only gate-passed articles. The corpus count and the pass rate are in the hover. They diverge sharply — the momentum beat passes at 31% against 3-8% elsewhere, because its atoms ARE the gate's vocabulary, so it is 17% of the corpus but 35% of everything the scout reads. Beats that retrieved articles but never produced a funded position sit at zero: they are pure cost. Read it against panel 5 — a tall bar there with a short bar here is a beat carried by volume rather than by quality.

8. Cumulative $ gain per event

The same gains grouped by the EVENT that motivated them. PWR groups this by wave bucket; GHR's unit of thesis is the event, so this is its analogue. It answers whether the curator's ideas paid, independently of which vehicle expressed them.

9. Portfolio value by event over time

How the book was distributed across events as the year ran. Wide bands that persist mean concentrated conviction; a churn of thin bands means the optimizer kept rotating.

10. Allocation over time

Dollars held per ticker, stacked — the top edge is the portfolio value. The always_include anchors (SPY, BIL) sit outside the watchlist cap and are where idle capital parks; a grey anchor stretch is the book in SPY/BIL, not a decision to hold cash. 221 of 753 days (29%) the book holds no position at all and sits in cash — drawn as its own band, not left blank. That is the optimizer cancelling trades, not the curator running out of ideas: at min_trade_size 0.1 with max_watchlist 8, positions sized below the floor are dropped rather than shrunk.

11. Thesis concentration

How much of the whole portfolio is riding on one event. Anchors are not a bet, so a day parked in SPY/BIL reads 0%; the dashed line is the per-ticker cap, for scale.

12. Curator funnel

Everything the curator touched, from the articles it read down to the picks it logged. Log x-axis. Two things to watch: the discovery gate is the largest cut in the whole pipeline (~19×), and it is scout-only — event agents still read the full window, so tracking an event is never starved.

Units change mid-funnel: admissions counts ticker-curations, so a ticker re-admitted in a later curation is counted again; distinct tickers and events are the de-duplicated views. NOT shown: the ticker guard, which resolves names to symbols and drops unresolvable ones before these counters see them.

13. Breadth over time

Events live, distinct tickers named, and how many separate catalysts those events represent — per rebalance. Several events on one theme is concentration wearing a diversity costume, which is why catalysts are drawn separately from events. The dashed line is max_watchlist = 8. Since the unfunded prune was turned on (2026-08-09) it binds in only 36 of 37 weeks — the prune keeps the live set under the cap by itself, so the cap is a backstop rather than an active knob. What used to sit between the solid and dashed lines was inventory the optimizer was never going to fund.

14. Scout inflow vs admissions

Candidate tickers the scout proposed each rebalance_period (30 days here), against what was admitted. Each candidate is a (ticker, thesis) pair, not an event — several can collapse into one event later (176 admissions became 179 events).

Nothing caps this: max_new_events is 0 (uncapped), superseded by max_events = 0, a concurrency cap applied later — so the gap between the bars is the already-resolved block and the ticker guard, not a knob.

15. Coverage vs picks, per ticker

Article counts for the 40 most-covered tickers in the corpus. Green got watchlisted at some point; grey was named in the news but never watchlisted.

16. Gain per article, per ticker

For the picked tickers above: dollars earned per article the press wrote about them. The per-ticker twin of plot 6. A name that paid a lot on little coverage sits far right; a heavily-covered loser sits far left. Only tickers that were both in the top-40 by coverage AND funded appear, so this is a subset of the bars above.

17. Evidence by lede provenance

For every article the curator cited as evidence, where its text came from. If picks cluster on archived text (Wayback, look-ahead-clean) the clean arm is earning its cost; if they cluster on live page text the corpus is leaning on look-ahead-biased material.

18. Evidence by source

Which outlets actually produced the articles behind the picks. Compare with the firehose dashboard's source panel: an outlet supplying much of the corpus but little of the evidence is volume without signal.

19. Evidence by beat

Which standing searches (retrieval_config.json) produced the articles behind the picks. A beat that fills the corpus but never appears here is paying rent without earning it.

20. Event storyboard

Each event's week-by-week journal: what the agent concluded, and why it eventually exited. The qualitative counterpart to the curation log — the only place you can see whether the exit logic is REASONING about a catalyst resolving or just pattern-matching on a price move. Funded events first, then those that never held capital.

21. Text provenance of what the curator read

Per week, how much of the pool reached the curator as archived text, live-page text, or a bare headline. This is the firehose's provenance panel restricted to the slices the curator actually read. Archived = Wayback (archive.org's snapshot as of the article's own date), which is the only look-ahead-CLEAN text here: a live page is fetched today and may have been edited, extended or corrected since publication, so it can carry knowledge the curator could not have had. A week leaning on live text is a week whose result is an upper bound.

22. Curation log

The 37 of 37 weekly calls that CHANGED something — a week where the curator opened or closed an event. No-change weeks are hidden. An event is one catalyst and the basket of tickers expressing it, so opening an event is GHR's analogue of an add. Proposed→admitted is what the scout put forward versus what survived the inflow cap, so a week where those differ is a week the cap bound.
